facts.claim: In a traditional Korean wedding the groom brings wooden geese to the bride's house in a ritual called jeonallye; live geese were used at first, and wooden geese began to replace them in the late Joseon period.
facts.quote: The groom brings wooden geese to the bride’s house in a ritual conducted as part of a traditional wedding, called jeonallye. At first live geese were used, but wooden geese started to replace live ones in the late Joseon period.

facts.claim: The V&A states that geese are a symbol of loyalty and fidelity and that wooden geese were used as a sign of the groom's everlasting love towards his bride.
facts.quote: Since geese are a symbol of loyalty and fidelity, wooden geese were used as a sign of the groom’s everlasting love towards his bride.

facts.claim: The V&A records the Korean wooden wedding duck or goose as 'kirogi' (older romanisation; gireogi in Revised Romanisation is not given by the source) and says presenting a live goose was borrowed from Chinese Confucian wedding ritual and survived in Korea long after it disappeared in China.
facts.quote: The presentation of a live goose was initially borrowed from Chinese Confucian wedding rituals and the custom survived in Korea long after it had disappeared in China. Over time real geese were substituted with wooden geese and ducks (in Korean, ‘kirogi’), supposedly because it was so difficult to obtain the former.

facts.claim: Britannica says Western dress has supplanted hanbok almost everywhere, but even urban dwellers still commonly wear it on special occasions including weddings, and there are different hanbok for special occasions such as weddings.
facts.quote: Western dress has supplanted the hanbok almost everywhere, but even urban dwellers commonly still wear it on special occasions such as important family meetings, holidays, weddings, and funerals. ... There are different hanbok for special occasions, such as weddings, babies’ birthdays, and 61st-birthday celebrations.

facts.claim: Britannica names marriage among the most important passages in a person's life in traditional Korean family life, alongside a baby's first 100 days and the 61st birthday.
facts.quote: The most important passages in a person’s life are the completion of a baby’s first 100 days, one’s marriage, and one’s 61st birthday.

facts.claim: The V&A records a wonsam (원삼) as a woman's ceremonial silk robe from Korea, about 1850 to 1950, with a green body, red ribbons and multi-coloured sleeves in red, yellow, blue, white and dark red.
facts.quote: Wonsam, Woman's ceremonial robe, made of silk in multi-coloured, Korea, ca.1850-1950 ... The woman's ceremonial robe, crafted from silk, a green body of the robe, adorned with red ribbons and showcasing multi-coloured sleeves in red, yellow, blue, white, and dark red.

facts.claim: The V&A records a woman's ceremonial robe ensemble titled Hwarot (활옷), made in Korea in the 1980s, comprising a red silk wonsam (robe) with flower-motif embroidery, a jeogori (jacket) and chima (skirts) with gold-leaf detailing.
facts.quote: Woman's ceremonial robe ensemble, comprising of wonsam (robe), jeogori (jacket), chima (skirts) ... features a red silk wonsam (robe) adorned with flower-motif embroidery, a light green silk jeogori (jacket), and suranchima (skirts) in blue and red hues with gold leaf detailing at the bottom.

facts.claim: Britannica describes women's formal hanbok as several layers of undergarments under a long, billowing skirt and short jacket closed with a long tie, and men's as full-legged pants and a long, wide-sleeved jacket.
facts.quote: Women’s and girls’ formal hanbok consists of several layers of undergarments under a colorful, long billowing skirt and short jacket held closed with a long tie. The men’s and boys’ version consists of full-legged pants and a long, wide-sleeved jacket.

insider_details.detail: If the couple include the wooden geese in a ceremony, the source-backed description is the groom bringing them to the bride's house in the jeonallye; the V&A gives loyalty and fidelity as the meaning, so the writer may state that meaning with a link, but not the 'mate for life' line as fact beyond the V&A wording.

Use 'jeonallye' (Revised Romanisation, as the V&A gives it) for the ritual; the V&A's 'kirogi' is an older romanisation, so 'gireogi' should be written as the Revised Romanisation without claiming a source spelled it that way.

Hanbok is still commonly worn for weddings even by city families, and there are dedicated wedding hanbok, so plan time in the schedule for a change of outfit between a Western-style ceremony and the traditional element.
Wonsam and hwarot are layered silk robes worn over a jeogori and chima; brief the photographer and the venue on extra dressing time and a clean, private room for the change.
